write_files:
  - path: /opt/decision-model/gpu-driver.sh
    permissions: "0755"
    content: |
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      set -euo pipefail
      # GPU plans boot without the NVIDIA driver. Install it once, then reboot;
      # the decision-model unit is enabled before this runs, so it resumes on boot.
      if lspci -nn | grep -qi nvidia; then
        if ! nvidia-smi >/dev/null 2>&1; then
          export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
          apt-get update -y
          apt-get install -y ubuntu-drivers-common
          ubuntu-drivers install --gpgpu || true
          if [ -f /var/lib/decision-model/rebooted ]; then
            echo "NVIDIA driver is still unavailable; the model runs on CPU" >&2
          else
            mkdir -p /var/lib/decision-model
            touch /var/lib/decision-model/rebooted
            reboot
          fi
        fi
      fi

  - path: /opt/decision-model/setup.sh
    permissions: "0755"
    content: |
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      set -euo pipefail
      export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

      if ! command -v ollama >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
      fi

      mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d
      cat > /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d/override.conf <<'EOF'
      [Service]
      Environment="OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:11434"
      Environment="OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=24h"
      EOF
      systemctl daemon-reload
      systemctl enable --now ollama

      # The first pull downloads several gigabytes, so retry rather than fail once.
      for attempt in $(seq 1 30); do
        if ollama pull ${model}; then
          break
        fi
        sleep 20
      done

      if ! command -v caddy >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        curl -1sLf https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/gpg.key \
          | gpg --batch --yes --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/caddy-stable-archive-keyring.gpg
        curl -1sLf https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/debian.deb.txt \
          > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/caddy-stable.list
        apt-get update -y
        apt-get install -y caddy
      fi

      # Ollama serves no authentication, so Caddy terminates TLS on a hostname
      # that resolves to this instance and requires the bearer token.
      domain="$(curl -fsS https://api.ipify.org).sslip.io"
      cat > /etc/caddy/Caddyfile <<EOF
      {
        email ${email}
      }
      https://$domain {
        @authed header Authorization "Bearer ${token}"
        handle @authed {
          reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:11434
        }
        respond 401
      }
      EOF
      systemctl enable caddy
      systemctl restart caddy

      ollama ps || true

  - path: /etc/systemd/system/decision-model.service
    content: |
      [Unit]
      Description=Self-hosted System One decision model
      Wants=network-online.target
      After=network-online.target ollama.service
      StartLimitIntervalSec=0

      [Service]
      Type=oneshot
      ExecStart=/opt/decision-model/setup.sh
      TimeoutStartSec=0

      [Install]
      WantedBy=multi-user.target

  - systemctl enable decision-model.service
  - bash /opt/decision-model/gpu-driver.sh
  - systemctl start decision-model.service

# Decision model on Vultr

A Vultr Cloud GPU instance running a Jev-compatible System One decision model
behind a token-protected HTTPS endpoint. The web app's audience scoring calls
`/v1/systemone` on it, so the decision model runs on Vultr rather than a hosted
API.

The instance installs NVIDIA drivers (rebooting once if needed), Ollama, the
model and Caddy from cloud-init. Caddy obtains a certificate for
`<ip>.sslip.io`, which resolves to the instance, and returns 401 unless the
request carries the bearer token. Ollama itself stays on localhost.

## Use

```sh
export VULTR_API_KEY=...          # console.vultr.com > API
tofu init
tofu plan
tofu apply
```

Then point the web app at it:

```sh
tofu output -raw url              # https://<ip>.sslip.io
tofu output -raw token            # sensitive
```

and set `SYSTEMONE_BASE_URL` and `SYSTEMONE_API_TOKEN` in `web/.env.local`.

The instance bills hourly from creation. Destroy it when the demo ends:

```sh
tofu destroy
```

## Plan choice

`plan` defaults to `vcg-a16-1c-6gb`, the cheapest NVIDIA plan with enough VRAM
for `clef-flash` (11–12 GB). List what the account can actually deploy:

```sh
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $VULTR_API_KEY" \
  'https://api.vultr.com/v2/plans?type=vcg' | jq '.plans[] | {id, gpu_type, gpu_vram, locations}'
```

Any CPU plan also works — Ollama falls back to CPU when no driver is present —
but a 9B model then takes tens of seconds per request instead of milliseconds.

so why is this adding all this networking, and how much is the cost etc

Fair challenge — most of that is optional. Here's what each piece is actually for, and what it costs.

## Why the networking exists

The thing we're deploying is Ollama, which has **no authentication at all**. If we bind it to `0.0.0.0:11434` and open the port, anyone on the internet can run inference on our bill. So there are three honest options:

| | What it needs | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Public HTTPS + token** (what I wrote) | Caddy, `sslip.io` hostname, rules for 80/443, 48-char bearer token | No manual step at demo time; the app can run from a laptop, Vercel, or anywhere. Adds ~10 lines of cloud-init. |
| **B. SSH tunnel** | Rule for 22 only; `ssh -N -L 11434:127.0.0.1:11434 root@<ip>` before the demo | Nothing is public; simplest stack. But the tunnel must be up for the whole demo, and it only works if the Next server runs on the same machine as the tunnel. |
| **C. Open port, no auth** | One firewall rule | Free and instant, and a bad idea. |

`sslip.io` is just free DNS that maps `<ip>.sslip.io` to the instance IP, so Caddy can get a real Let's Encrypt certificate without buying a domain. The firewall group is Vultr's, created by the same `apply`, so it's four rules in code rather than clicking in a console.

Since the demo currently runs locally (there's no `.vercel` link or `web/.env.local`, so nothing is deployed), **B is genuinely sufficient**. I chose A because it removes a pre-demo command and keeps the option of deploying the app later. If you want less machinery, B cuts Caddy, the token, the ACME email and two firewall rules, and I'd rewrite cloud-init accordingly — about 15 minutes of work, less than the current version.

| Plan | Hourly | 3 hours (apply ~now → destroy after demo) | If left running a month |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A16, 1×16 GB** (default; fits `clef-flash` at 11–12 GB) | $0.471/h | **~$1.41** | ~$315–344 |
| L40S, 1×48 GB | $1.671/h | ~$5.01 | ~$1,120 |
| 8 vCPU / 16 GB CPU-only (High Performance AMD) | $0.143/h | ~$0.43 | ~$96 |

Inbound bandwidth (the 11 GB model download) is inside the 6 TB allowance, so it adds nothing. Sign-up credits are $250–300, so any of these is effectively free — but the real risk is **forgetting to `tofu destroy`**, because a stopped instance still bills. That's the one operational cost worth naming: a leaked instance is ~$11/day.

So: GPU provisioning is a couple of pounds at most; the price is the 10–15 minutes of provisioning plus the demo dependency, not the money.

input.newString: - Audience fit scoring: a decision model scores the target-customer sentence against each column of the prebuilt tract dataset, and the web app weights the columns by those scores. The model answers declared yes/no, choice and score questions with probabilities instead of writing text. Clef-flash, a 9B System One model, runs on a Vultr Cloud Compute instance managed by OpenTofu in `infra/vultr/` and is called over `/v1/systemone` when `SYSTEMONE_BASE_URL` is set. Jev through AI Gateway answers the same request when the self-hosted endpoint fails, and keyword weights answer it when neither is reachable; the Customers tab names which one ran. The tract data is numbers, which code combines without a model, so the model's part is turning the sentence into weights. Weights are signed, because the direction depends on the customer: a high income is good for an affluent audience and bad for a low-income one, and `median_age` points the opposite way for young and older audiences. The weighted score divides by the sum of the absolute weights, because signed weights can sum to zero and make a plain average unstable. 2026-11-08.

**Money:** credit confirmed ($100), spend so far ≈ $0.05; the instance is $0.59 for a 3-hour window, ~$144/month if left running.

## The decision, and there are only two real ones

**A. Put the app on Vultr instead of the model.** The challenge says "runs on Vultr (cloud compute **or** cloud GPUs)". A Next.js deployment on this instance qualifies, is checkable by a judge, and doesn't depend on inference speed. Scoring would use Jev if a Gateway key exists, keywords otherwise; the model endpoint stays live but unused. ~25–35 min. This is my recommendation.

**B. Keep the model in the live path.** Switch the app to `tev1:4b` and raise the timeout to ~90s. Smaller model, still ~30–60s per submission on this CPU, visibly stalled form. Demoable, not good.

input.content:
# Decision model on Vultr

A Vultr instance running a Jev-compatible System One decision model behind a
token-protected HTTPS endpoint. The web app's audience scoring calls
`/v1/systemone` on it, so the decision model runs on Vultr rather than a hosted
API.

Cloud-init installs Docker, pulls `ollama/ollama` from Docker Hub (Ollama's own
installer downloads from GitHub releases, which rate-limits), pulls the models,
and runs Caddy. Caddy obtains a certificate for `<ip>.sslip.io`, which resolves
to the instance, returns 401 unless the request carries the bearer token, and
proxies to Ollama on localhost. Ubuntu's firewall only allows SSH, HTTP and
HTTPS.

## Use

```sh
export VULTR_API_KEY=...          # console.vultr.com > API
tofu init
tofu plan
tofu apply
```

Then point the web app at it:

```sh
tofu output -raw url              # https://<ip>.sslip.io
tofu output -raw token            # sensitive
```

and set `SYSTEMONE_BASE_URL` and `SYSTEMONE_API_TOKEN` in `web/.env.local`.

The instance bills hourly from creation. Destroy it when the demo ends:

```sh
tofu destroy
```

Changing `user_data` replaces the instance, because Vultr only runs it at first
boot.

## Plans

`plan` defaults to `vhp-12c-24gb-amd`, a 12-vCPU, 24 GB CPU instance at
$0.197/h. It runs a 9B model in about 24 tokens per second of prompt
processing: a single question takes seconds, but the 21-question audience
request takes a couple of minutes, so this plan is for proving the setup rather
than for a fast demo.

A GPU plan is the same stack: set `plan` to a `vcg-*` ID and the cloud-init
installs the NVIDIA driver and reboots once before starting the model. Check
what the account can actually deploy, because a plan the account is not enabled
for is listed with an empty `locations` list:

```sh
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $VULTR_API_KEY" \
  'https://api.vultr.com/v2/plans?type=vcg' | jq '.plans[] | {id, gpu_type, gpu_vram, locations}'
for r in $(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $VULTR_API_KEY" \
  'https://api.vultr.com/v2/regions?per_page=500' | jq -r '.regions[].id'); do
  echo "$r: $(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $VULTR_API_KEY" \
    "https://api.vultr.com/v2/regions/$r/availability?type=vcg" | jq -r '.available_plans[]?' | tr '\n' ' ')"
done
```

The model answers declared yes/no, choice and score questions with probabilities instead of writing text. A System One model runs on a Vultr Cloud Compute instance managed by OpenTofu in `infra/vultr/` and is called over `/v1/systemone` when `SYSTEMONE_BASE_URL` is set; the demo uses `tev1:4b` because the 9B `clef-flash` is slower on CPU, and both are pulled. Jev through AI Gateway answers the same request when the self-hosted endpoint fails, and keyword weights answer it when neither is reachable; the Customers tab names which one ran. The tract data is numbers, which code combines without a model, so the model's part is turning the sentence into weights. Weights are signed, because the direction depends on the customer: a high income is good for an affluent audience and bad for a low-income one, and `median_age` points the opposite way for young and older audiences. The weighted score divides by the sum of the absolute weights, because signed weights can sum to zero and make a plain average unstable. 2026-11-08.

Added and live.

- The Customers tab now shows a thin accent-coloured bar that fills against the usual 90 seconds, with `Scoring 2,324 census tracts with the self-hosted model… 47s of about 90` beside it.
- It deliberately stops at 97%: the endpoint returns nothing until the whole request finishes, so real progress isn't available, and a bar that sits at 100% while still waiting would be worse than one that sits short.
- It carries `role="progressbar"` with the elapsed percentage, so it reads correctly to assistive tech.
- The after-run line is unchanged: `tev1:4b answered 21 traits in 126.6 s from 5,189 input tokens on Vultr CPU.`

Deployed to `https://app.45.32.178.114.sslip.io`, and `localhost:3000` has it through hot reload. Committed as `fc0cd00` and pushed; 51 tests, lint, typecheck and build pass. (Running the tests from the repo root makes 12 fail on relative data paths — they read `../data` from their own cwd — which is pre-existing, not this change.)

Worth one dry run on the hosted copy before 12:00: submit, watch the bar, and check the stats line lands. The instance is still billing at $0.197/h; say the word after the demo and I'll `tofu destroy` it.
do you think we could get it that the map fills in gradually rather than waiting

Yes — but the honest version costs real plumbing, and there are two very different ways to get it. Both are feasible; the difference is what a judge sees.

**A. Genuinely gradual (the good version).** Split the 21 traits into three batches of seven, stream a `weights + tract scores` event after each batch, and repaint the map when each arrives. Prompt size per batch drops to about a third, so the first map appears around 25–30 s and refines at ~55 s and ~90 s. It needs a new streaming Route Handler like the one competitor research already uses, plus reworking `use-audience-run` and the run state so partial fits are valid. **60–75 minutes including deploy and one verification run**, and it touches the demo's critical path.

**B. Instant provisional map (the safe version).** Paint the map immediately from keyword weights, label it "provisional", and swap to the model's weights when they land (~25–35 min). No blank screen, but not gradual — and during a demo the colours visibly change once, which can read as the tool changing its mind unless the label is prominent.

**C. Keep the progress bar.** Honest, zero risk, and the stats line already tells the story of a 90-second CPU score.

My recommendation: **A now** if you're comfortable with me touching the scoring path with about 90 minutes left, because it's the version that actually looks good and it's the same architecture we'd want anyway. The risk is bounded: if it's not working by about 11:30 I revert to C, since the current path is committed and deployed.

input.newString: - Audience fit scoring: a decision model scores the target-customer sentence against each column of the prebuilt tract dataset, and the web app weights the columns by those scores. The model answers declared yes/no, choice and score questions with probabilities instead of writing text. A System One model runs on a Vultr Cloud Compute instance managed by OpenTofu in `infra/vultr/` and is called over `/v1/systemone` when `SYSTEMONE_BASE_URL` is set; the demo uses `tev1:4b` because the 9B `clef-flash` is slower on CPU, and both are pulled. The columns are asked in three batches of seven, streamed from a Route Handler, so the map can be scored and drawn after the first batch and refined twice. Jev through AI Gateway answers the same request when the self-hosted endpoint fails, and keyword weights answer it when neither is reachable; the Customers tab names which one ran. The tract data is numbers, which code combines without a model, so the model's part is turning the sentence into weights. Weights are signed, because the direction depends on the customer: a high income is good for an affluent audience and bad for a low-income one, and `median_age` points the opposite way for young and older audiences. The weighted score divides by the sum of the absolute weights, because signed weights can sum to zero and make a plain average unstable. 2026-11-08.
